title: For a given number N, generate all combinations of N pairs of balanced parentheses. Explain the backtracking technique that tracks open and close counts to keep every prefix valid.
keyPoints: Backtrack with openCount and closeCount: place '(' while openCount < N, place ')' while closeCount < openCount.
The closeCount < openCount invariant keeps every prefix valid, so no filtering is needed.
The number of valid combinations is the Nth Catalan number, far fewer than 2^(2N) brute-force candidates.
Use StringBuilder with append-recurse-deleteCharAt for efficient in-place backtracking.
This generate-only-valid technique avoids all wasted work on invalid candidates.
The Catalan number also counts binary trees and polygon triangulations, signaling mathematical depth.

s1_definition.oneliner: Backtrack placing an open while opens are below N, and a close only while closes trail opens, recording at length 2N.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Balanced Parentheses** – generate all valid strings of N open and N close parentheses using constrained backtracking.
- **Two placement rules** – append `(` while `openCount < N`; append `)` only while `closeCount < openCount`.
- **Invariant** – `closeCount < openCount` ensures every prefix has at least as many opens as closes.
- **Count** – the number of valid results is the Nth Catalan number.
- **Backtracking** – append one character, recurse with updated counts, then delete the character to undo.
- **No filtering** – every string built is valid by construction.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, nested approval brackets must open and close in balance. For N levels, the governance team wants every valid bracketing. A designer writes the pattern left to right: she can open a new bracket as long as she has brackets left, and she can close one only if there is an unclosed bracket waiting. Every pattern she writes is automatically valid.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Backtracking Tree for N=2
  ──────────────────────────

                ""
               /
              (
            /   \
          ((     ()
          |      |
         (()    ()(
          |      |
         (())   ()()

  Results: "(())", "()()"
```

```text
  Decision at each node:
  ──────────────────────
  Can place '('?  → openCount < N
  Can place ')'?  → closeCount < openCount
  Done?           → length == 2N → record
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Balanced Parentheses generates all valid combinations of N pairs using constrained backtracking. I build the string character by character with two counters, placing an open while `openCount < N` and a close only while `closeCount < openCount`. The `closeCount < openCount` invariant guarantees every prefix stays valid, so every leaf is a correct result with no post-generation filtering.

The count of results is the Nth Catalan number, which grows far slower than the 2^(2N) brute-force candidates. For N=10, that is 16796 valid strings versus over a million. Using `StringBuilder` with append-recurse-deleteCharAt keeps the backtracking efficient without string allocation overhead.

This constrained generation technique, where validity rules act as pruning, is a general optimization pattern that applies to Sudoku, N-Queens, and expression generation. Recognizing the Catalan number connection signals mathematical depth to an interviewer.

At the National Bank of India, I used this to enumerate all valid nested approval workflow shapes for governance review. Each generated template was valid by construction, saving reviewers from examining nonsensical patterns. Explaining the two placement rules, why they keep every prefix valid, and the Catalan count is what shows an interviewer I understand backtracking with invariants.

Remember one sentence: place an open while budget remains, place a close only while closes trail opens, and every string is valid by construction.
